course.description: Meet the particles, build a bond and keep every atom. Predict how much a reaction can make.

lessons.title: What makes an element?

blocks.text: Count the centre
An element is identified by its proton count. That count is its atomic number, Z. Oxygen has eight protons even when its neutrons or electrons change.
Keep the identity
A neutron adds to the nucleus without changing the element. An electron changes charge without changing the nucleus.
Balance the charge
A proton carries one positive charge and an electron one negative charge. A neutral atom has equal numbers of the two.
Read the symbol
Al is the symbol for aluminium. Its atomic number is 13, so any aluminium atom has thirteen protons. The symbol does not specify its neutron count.

lessons.orientation: Use protons to identify an element and separate identity from mass and charge.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

lessons.title: Same element, different mass

blocks.text: Add the nucleus
Mass number A counts protons plus neutrons in one nucleus. Carbon with six protons and seven neutrons is carbon-13.
Find the missing count
Subtract atomic number from mass number to find neutrons: N = A − Z. Electron loss does not change mass number.
Compare isotopes
Isotopes share a proton count but have different neutron counts. They belong to one element, though their masses differ.
Average a sample
An average describes many atoms. For an equal mixture with approximate masses 12 u and 14 u, the average is 13 u; no atom in that mixture needs to have mass 13 u.

lessons.orientation: Distinguish mass number, isotopes and the average mass of a mixture.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

lessons.title: Gaining and losing electrons

blocks.text: One electron short
Charge in units of the elementary charge is protons minus electrons. Sodium with eleven protons and ten electrons is Na⁺.
Extra negative charge
An oxygen atom that gains two electrons has ten electrons against eight protons. Its charge is −2, written O²⁻.
Change the electrons
Removing a negative electron makes charge more positive. Ordinary chemical ion formation does not remove protons.
Three missing negatives
Aluminium commonly forms Al³⁺ by losing three electrons. Its proton count stays thirteen and its electron count becomes ten.

lessons.orientation: Calculate ion charge while keeping element identity unchanged.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

lessons.title: The outer electrons

blocks.text: Look outside
For neutral ground-state atoms up to argon, group electrons as 2 in the first shell, then up to 8 in the second and up to 8 in the third. Oxygen's eight electrons group as 2, 6.
Fill a shell
Neon has ten electrons: two inner and eight outer. The outer electrons are called valence electrons; their arrangement helps explain chemical behaviour.
Start another shell
Sodium has eleven electrons: 2, 8, 1. Its single outer electron occupies a new shell. The circles group counts; electrons do not travel along these drawn tracks.
Keep the first exception
Helium's first shell is full with two electrons. A full outer shell does not always mean eight, and larger atoms require a more detailed orbital model.

lessons.orientation: Read shell populations for the first eighteen elements and identify valence electrons.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

lessons.title: Making a neutral formula

blocks.text: Cancel the charge
One Mg²⁺ needs two Cl⁻ ions to balance charge: +2 − 1 − 1 = 0. The simplest neutral ratio gives MgCl₂.
Meet at six
Two Al³⁺ ions supply +6 and three O²⁻ ions supply −6. This gives the formula Al₂O₃. Each subscript counts ions in the simplest ratio.
Think lattice
An ionic crystal extends through many ions. Its formula unit gives a ratio, not a separate molecule floating inside the solid.
Reduce the ratio
Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ cancel in a one-to-one ratio, so write MgO. Two of each also balance, but Mg₂O₂ is not the simplest formula unit.

lessons.orientation: Find whole-number ion ratios that balance electric charge.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

lessons.title: Sharing electron pairs

blocks.text: Share a pair
A single covalent bond represents two shared electrons. In H₂, both hydrogen atoms count that pair toward a filled first shell.
Use two pairs
A double bond contains two shared pairs: four electrons. In a Lewis structure, O₂ has a double bond and two lone pairs on each oxygen.
Count shared electrons once
The same bonding pair contributes to each bonded atom's shell count. It remains two electrons in the molecule; counting it for both atoms does not create four.
Three lines
A triple bond contains three shared pairs, or six electrons. N₂ also has one lone pair on each nitrogen. Lewis drawings show electron bookkeeping, not a complete three-dimensional shape.

lessons.orientation: Read single, double and triple bonds and distinguish shared electrons from lone pairs.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

lessons.title: Reading a chemical formula

blocks.text: Count whole units
H₂O means two H atoms and one O atom per water molecule. A coefficient multiplies the whole formula, so 3 H₂O contains six H atoms and three O atoms.
Multiply every element
Al₂O₃ gives a two-to-three ratio of aluminium to oxygen. Two formula units contain four aluminium atoms and six oxygen atoms.
Keep a substance intact
Changing a coefficient changes the amount. Changing a subscript changes the formula and may describe a different substance.
Read the invisible one
NH₃ contains one nitrogen and three hydrogen atoms. A missing subscript means one. Five molecules contain five N atoms and fifteen H atoms.

lessons.orientation: Separate subscripts inside a formula from coefficients multiplying whole units.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

lessons.title: Adding atomic masses

blocks.text: Weigh a formula
For these estimates use H = 1 u, C = 12 u, N = 14 u and O = 16 u. Water's formula mass is 2 × 1 + 16 = 18 u.
Count repeated atoms
A CO₂ molecule contains one carbon and two oxygen atoms. Using C = 12 u and O = 16 u gives 12 + 2 × 16 = 44 u.
Use the stated precision
Rounded atomic masses are estimates for this course's arithmetic. They do not turn average atomic masses into exact integer measurements.
Count a formula unit
Ionic solids also have formula masses. With Mg = 24 u and Cl = 35.5 u, MgCl₂ has formula mass 24 + 2 × 35.5 = 95 u.

lessons.orientation: Build formula mass from atom counts and stated rounded atomic masses.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

lessons.title: From moles to mass

blocks.text: Count an enormous group
A mole contains exactly 6.02214076 × 10²³ specified entities. One mole of H₂O counts water molecules; one mole of NaCl counts formula units.
Use grams per mole
Molar mass M converts amount n to mass m: m = nM. With M(H₂O) = 18 g/mol, two moles have mass 36 g.
Reverse the conversion
To find amount from mass, divide by molar mass: n = m/M. For CO₂ at 44 g/mol, 22 g corresponds to 0.5 mol.
Count atoms within molecules
One mole of NH₃ molecules contains three moles of H atoms and one mole of N atoms. The subscript ratio works for molecules and for moles.

lessons.orientation: Convert between amount and mass while identifying what one mole counts.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

lessons.title: Keep every atom

blocks.text: Match each element
A balanced chemical equation has the same count of each element on both sides. In 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O, four H atoms and two O atoms are conserved.
Check all the oxygen
For CH₄ + 2 O₂ → CO₂ + 2 H₂O, count oxygen in both products: two atoms in CO₂ and two more in the waters.
Leave formulas alone
A coefficient changes the number of molecules or formula units. Changing H₂O to H₂O₂ would replace water with a different substance, not balance the same reaction.
Match hydrogen last
N₂ + 3 H₂ → 2 NH₃ has two N atoms and six H atoms on each side. Balanced coefficients can be multiplied together, but the simplest whole-number ratio is usually used.

lessons.orientation: Balance reactions by changing coefficients while preserving chemical formulas.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

lessons.title: Read a reaction as a ratio

blocks.text: Scale the recipe
N₂ + 3 H₂ → 2 NH₃ means one mole of nitrogen requires three moles of hydrogen and can form two moles of ammonia. Scale all amounts together.
Follow the ratio
The equation 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O gives a 1:2 ratio between oxygen and water. With enough hydrogen, each mole of O₂ can produce two moles of water.
Keep the units
Equation coefficients give particle and mole ratios. They do not generally give mass ratios, because substances have different molar masses.
Read the direction
CH₄ + 2 O₂ → CO₂ + 2 H₂O needs two moles of oxygen per mole of methane. The conversion factor depends on which substance you start with and which you want.

lessons.orientation: Use balanced coefficients to convert between reacting and produced amounts.
lessons.reviewLabel: Read a reaction as a ratio
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

lessons.title: The reactant that runs out

blocks.text: Find the smaller batch count
For 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O, six moles of H₂ could support three batches, but one mole of O₂ supports only one. Oxygen limits the product to two moles of water.
Compare after dividing
For N₂ + 3 H₂ → 2 NH₃, divide each supply by its coefficient. Four moles of N₂ support four batches; three moles of H₂ support one. Hydrogen runs out first.
Keep the leftovers
An excess reactant is not all consumed. In the water case with 6 mol H₂ and 1 mol O₂, forming 2 mol H₂O consumes 2 mol H₂ and leaves 4 mol H₂.
Transfer the method
With 3 mol CH₄ and 4 mol O₂, CH₄ + 2 O₂ → CO₂ + 2 H₂O can proceed through two molar batches. It forms 2 mol CO₂ and 4 mol H₂O, leaving 1 mol CH₄.

lessons.orientation: Find theoretical products and leftovers by comparing available amounts with the reaction ratio.

questions.prompt: Oxygen has 8 protons, 8 neutrons and 8 electrons. What is its atomic number?
hints: Choose the particle that identifies the element.
Z counts protons; it ignores neutrons and electrons.
Which supplied count is the definition of atomic number?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Atomic number counts protons, so Z = 8.

questions.prompt: The two carbon cases differ in neutron count. Why are they both carbon?
hints: Compare the nuclei's proton counts.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Each nucleus still contains six protons.

questions.prompt: A neutral nitrogen atom has 7 protons. How many electrons does it have?
hints: Neutral means no net electric charge.
Match the positive and negative particle counts.
Which electron count cancels every positive charge?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Seven electrons cancel the charge of seven protons.

questions.prompt: Aluminium has atomic number 13. How many protons does an aluminium ion contain?
hints: An ion retains its element's nucleus.
Ion formation changes electrons, not the atomic number.
Read the stated atomic number without adjusting it for ion charge.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Ion formation changes electrons, so its thirteen protons remain.

questions.prompt: Which change makes a carbon atom an atom of a different element?
hints: Distinguish identity from charge and mass.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Changing the proton count changes the atomic number.

questions.prompt: A fluorine nucleus contains 9 protons and 10 neutrons. How many particles are in its nucleus?
hints: Leave electrons out of the nucleus count.
The nucleus contains the two massive particle types.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Only protons and neutrons are in the nucleus: 9 + 10 = 19.

questions.prompt: A carbon nucleus has 6 protons and 7 neutrons. What is its mass number?
hints: Add the particles in the nucleus.
Use A = protons + neutrons.
Add 6 + 7.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Mass number is 6 + 7 = 13.

questions.prompt: Chlorine-35 has atomic number 17. How many neutrons does it have?
hints: Use N = A − Z.
Mass number counts protons and neutrons together.
Subtract 17 from 35.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Subtract 17 protons from mass number 35: 18 neutrons.

questions.prompt: Oxygen-16 and oxygen-18 are isotopes. What differs?
hints: Compare mass numbers while holding atomic number fixed.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Both have eight protons; oxygen-18 has two more neutrons.

questions.prompt: A sample has equal numbers of atoms of approximate mass 12 u and 14 u. What is its average mass in u?
hints: Give the two masses equal weight.
Half the atoms contribute each mass.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Equal populations give (12 + 14)/2 = 13 u.

questions.prompt: An oxygen-18 ion still has 8 protons. How many neutrons does it have?
hints: The ion's electron count is irrelevant here.
The nucleus has mass number 18 and proton count 8.
Subtract 8 from 18.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Charge does not affect mass number: 18 − 8 = 10.

questions.prompt: An element's average atomic mass is 10.8 u. What does this tell you?
hints: Separate a sample average from one atom's mass number.

acceptedIdeas: Its isotope mixture has that average mass
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A weighted average can be non-integer even though each nucleus has whole particles.

choices.label: Every atom has a fractional neutron
Its atoms all have mass number 11
Its isotope mixture has that average mass

questions.prompt: A sodium ion has 11 protons and 10 electrons. Enter its signed charge.
hints: Count positive charges minus negative charges.
Use charge = proton count − electron count.
Calculate 11 − 10.

questions.prompt: An oxide ion has 8 protons and 10 electrons. Enter its signed charge.
hints: More electrons than protons gives negative charge.
Subtract all ten negative charges from eight positive charges.
Calculate 8 − 10, keeping the sign.

questions.prompt: What happens when a neutral atom loses one electron?
hints: The nucleus stays unchanged.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Removing a negative charge leaves a net positive charge.

questions.prompt: An aluminium ion has 13 protons and 10 electrons. Enter its signed charge.
hints: Subtract electrons from protons.
There are three more protons than electrons.
Calculate 13 − 10.

questions.prompt: A fluoride ion has 9 protons and 10 electrons. Enter its signed charge.
hints: One extra electron contributes one negative charge.
Electrons outnumber protons by one.
Calculate 9 − 10, keeping the sign.

questions.prompt: Mg²⁺ and a neutral magnesium atom share what?
hints: Identity follows the nucleus.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Both have twelve protons; Mg²⁺ has two fewer electrons.

questions.prompt: Neutral oxygen has 8 electrons. With 2 in its first shell, how many are in its outer shell?
hints: Remove the filled first shell from the total.
Only the first shell is inside the outer shell for oxygen.
Calculate 8 − 2.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 8 − 2 = 6 outer electrons.

questions.prompt: Neutral neon has 10 electrons. How many valence electrons does it have?
hints: Identify the outermost occupied shell.
Two of neon's electrons belong to its first shell.
Calculate 10 − 2.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Its shell counts are 2, 8.

questions.prompt: Lithium has shell counts 2, 1 and sodium has 2, 8, 1. What matches?
hints: Compare the last occupied shell.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Each has one electron in its outermost shell.

questions.prompt: How many electrons fill helium's only shell?
hints: Helium occupies the first shell only.
The first shell holds a maximum of two electrons.
Count the pair in helium's only shell.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The first shell is full with two electrons.

questions.prompt: Neutral aluminium has 13 electrons arranged 2, 8, 3. How many are valence electrons?
hints: Use the final occupied group.
Ignore the two inner occupied groups.
Read the population of the last occupied shell.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The outermost occupied shell contains three.

questions.prompt: What do the circles in this atom drawing represent?
hints: Use the drawing as a model of shell populations.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: They group electrons for counting; actual electrons occupy quantum states.

questions.prompt: How many Cl⁻ ions balance one Mg²⁺ ion?
hints: Make the total charge zero.
Read the positive ion's charge before counting negative ions.
How many single negative charges cancel the magnesium charge?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two charges of −1 balance +2.

questions.prompt: In Al₂O₃, how many Al³⁺ ions accompany three O²⁻ ions?
hints: Find the positive count needed to reach +6.
Three oxide ions contribute −6 altogether.
Divide the required positive charge 6 by 3 per aluminium ion.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Three oxide ions total −6; two aluminium ions total +6.

questions.prompt: What does NaCl describe in a sodium chloride crystal?
hints: Distinguish a formula unit from a molecular structure.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: NaCl records the simplest ratio of sodium and chloride ions in a lattice.

choices.label: Two neutral atoms with no attraction

questions.prompt: In the simplest formula MgO, how many oxide ions accompany one magnesium ion?
hints: Compare the sizes of the opposite charges.
One magnesium and one oxide have equal and opposite charges.
Use the smallest positive whole-number count that cancels +2.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: +2 and −2 cancel one to one.

questions.prompt: Calcium forms Ca²⁺. How many Cl⁻ ions are needed per calcium ion?
hints: Balance charge using whole ions.
Each chloride cancels one unit of positive charge.
How many single negative charges cancel the calcium charge?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two chloride ions supply a total of −2.

questions.prompt: Why does aluminium oxide use the ratio Al₂O₃?
hints: Count net charge rather than guessed neighbours.

acceptedIdeas: It makes the total charge zero
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Two +3 charges balance three −2 charges.

choices.label: It makes the total charge zero
Every ion must have three neighbours
Oxygen changes to a positive ion

questions.prompt: How many electrons are shared in the single bond of H₂?
hints: Count two electrons per shared pair.
A single line means one shared pair.
How many electrons make one pair?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: One bonding pair contains two electrons.

questions.prompt: How many electrons are shared in the double bond of O₂?
hints: Each bond line represents one pair.
A double bond has two shared pairs.
Multiply 2 pairs by 2 electrons per pair.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two pairs contain four shared electrons.

questions.prompt: How does a shared pair contribute to the two bonded atoms?
hints: Keep shell counting separate from the total electron count.

acceptedIdeas: Each atom counts the pair toward its shell
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A shared pair counts toward both shells while remaining one pair in the molecule.

choices.label: Each atom counts the pair toward its shell
Each atom receives two new extra electrons
Only the heavier atom counts the pair

questions.prompt: How many electrons are shared in the triple bond of N₂?
hints: Multiply the number of lines by two.
A triple bond has three shared pairs.
Multiply 3 pairs by 2 electrons per pair.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Three shared pairs contain six electrons.

questions.prompt: NH₃ has one lone pair on nitrogen. How many nonbonding electrons is that?
hints: A lone pair is not a bond line.
The prompt gives one lone pair.
How many electrons make one pair?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A lone pair contains two electrons.

questions.prompt: Methane is drawn with four bonds on a flat screen. What can you infer from this Lewis drawing?
hints: Read bond connections without treating screen angles as measurements.

acceptedIdeas: It has four single C–H bonds
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The diagram records four single bonds; it does not specify the real tetrahedral geometry.

choices.label: Its atoms must all lie in one plane
It has four single C–H bonds
Its bond angles must be 90 degrees

questions.prompt: How many oxygen atoms are in 3 H₂O molecules?
hints: Multiply the O subscript, which is one, by the coefficient.
Each H₂O contains one O atom.
Each water contributes one oxygen; count the water molecules.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each molecule has one oxygen: 3 × 1 = 3.

questions.prompt: How many oxygen atoms are represented by 2 Al₂O₃ formula units?
hints: Multiply the entire formula by two.
The O subscript is three.
Multiply 2 formula units by 3 O atoms per unit.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each unit has three O atoms: 2 × 3 = 6.

questions.prompt: To double an amount of water without changing the substance, what do you change?
hints: Keep the formula of each molecule fixed.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A coefficient multiplies whole water molecules.

questions.prompt: How many hydrogen atoms are in 5 NH₃ molecules?
hints: Each ammonia molecule contributes three H atoms.
The H subscript is three.
Multiply 5 molecules by 3 H atoms per molecule.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 5 × 3 = 15 hydrogen atoms.

questions.prompt: How many chlorine atoms are represented by 4 MgCl₂ formula units?
hints: Apply the coefficient to chlorine too.
The Cl subscript is two.
Multiply 4 formula units by 2 Cl atoms per unit.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each unit contributes two Cl atoms: 4 × 2 = 8.

questions.prompt: What does 2 H₂ represent?
hints: Read the outside number separately from the inside number.

acceptedIdeas: Two molecules with two H atoms each
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The coefficient counts molecules and the subscript counts atoms per molecule.

choices.label: One molecule with four bonded H atoms
Two molecules with two H atoms each

questions.prompt: Using H = 1 u and O = 16 u, find the formula mass of H₂O in u.
hints: Add both hydrogens before adding oxygen.
Count two H atoms and one O atom.
Evaluate 2 × 1 + 16.

questions.prompt: Using C = 12 u and O = 16 u, find the formula mass of CO₂ in u.
hints: There are two oxygen atoms.
Count one C atom and two O atoms.
Evaluate 12 + 2 × 16.

questions.prompt: Why must you use the atomic masses stated in a problem?
hints: Distinguish rounded estimates from precise tabulated masses.

acceptedIdeas: The stated values set the intended approximation
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Using the same stated precision keeps the calculation consistent.

choices.label: All isotope masses are exact integers
The stated values set the intended approximation
Atomic mass depends on the size of the drawing

questions.prompt: Using Mg = 24 u and Cl = 35.5 u, find the formula mass of MgCl₂ in u.
hints: The subscript multiplies chlorine's mass.
Add one magnesium mass and two chlorine masses.
Evaluate 24 + 2 × 35.5.

questions.prompt: Using N = 14 u and H = 1 u, find the formula mass of NH₃ in u.
hints: The missing subscript after N means one.
Add one nitrogen mass and three hydrogen masses.
Evaluate 14 + 3 × 1.

questions.prompt: Which operation finds the mass of one CO₂ molecule from atomic masses?
hints: Count each atom's contribution.

acceptedIdeas: Add one C mass and twice the O mass
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Formula mass sums the masses of the atoms present.

choices.label: Average the masses of C and O
Add one C mass and twice the O mass
Multiply C mass by O mass

questions.prompt: Using M(H₂O) = 18 g/mol, find the mass of 2 mol of water in grams.
hints: Multiply the amount by grams per mole.
Each mole of this water estimate has mass 18 g.
Evaluate 2 × 18.

questions.prompt: What does one mole of H₂O count?
hints: Read the formula after the amount unit.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The specified entities are water molecules.

choices.label: Only oxygen atoms separated from water

questions.prompt: Using M(CO₂) = 44 g/mol, how many moles are in 22 g of CO₂?
hints: Divide mass by grams per mole.
Use amount = mass divided by molar mass.
The given mass is what fraction of one mole's mass?

questions.prompt: How many moles of H atoms are contained in 2 mol of NH₃ molecules?
hints: Apply the subscript to the molar amount.
One mole of NH₃ contains three moles of H atoms.
Evaluate 2 × 3.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each NH₃ contains three H atoms: 2 × 3 = 6 mol H atoms.

questions.prompt: Using M(CH₄) = 16 g/mol, find the mass of 3 mol of methane in grams.
hints: Use m = nM.
Each mole of methane has the stated mass 16 g.
Evaluate 3 × 16.

questions.prompt: Equal moles of water and carbon dioxide have what in common?
hints: Compare counts before comparing masses.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The mole counts entities; the different molecules have different molar masses.

choices.label: Equal numbers of atoms per molecule

questions.prompt: Balance 2 H₂ + ? O₂ → 2 H₂O. What coefficient belongs before O₂?
hints: Count oxygen atoms on both sides.
Two waters contain two oxygen atoms.
Divide the two required O atoms by two atoms per O₂.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two waters contain two O atoms, supplied by one O₂.

questions.prompt: Balance CH₄ + ? O₂ → CO₂ + 2 H₂O. What coefficient belongs before O₂?
hints: Include the oxygen inside water.
CO₂ has two O atoms and two waters have two more.
Divide the total four O atoms by two per O₂.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The products contain four O atoms, so two O₂ molecules are needed.

questions.prompt: What may you change while balancing a fixed chemical reaction?
hints: Preserve every substance's formula.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Coefficients adjust quantities without changing substances.

questions.prompt: Balance N₂ + ? H₂ → 2 NH₃. What coefficient belongs before H₂?
hints: Each H₂ provides two hydrogen atoms.
Two ammonias have six H atoms altogether.
Divide six H atoms by two per H₂.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two NH₃ molecules contain six H atoms, supplied by three H₂.

questions.prompt: Balance 2 Mg + O₂ → ? MgO. What coefficient belongs before MgO?
hints: Count each element separately.
Each MgO contains one Mg and one O.
Match both given magnesium atoms with one MgO unit each.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two MgO formula units preserve both Mg atoms and both O atoms.

questions.prompt: What must a balanced equation conserve?
hints: Compare element counts rather than total molecules.

acceptedIdeas: The count of each element's atoms
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Atoms rearrange; the number of molecules may change.

choices.label: The number of molecules on each side
The count of each element's atoms
The volume of every gas separately

questions.prompt: For N₂ + 3 H₂ → 2 NH₃, how many moles of NH₃ can 2 mol N₂ form with excess H₂?
hints: Use the ammonia-to-nitrogen coefficient ratio.
The equation gives two ammonia moles per nitrogen mole.
Evaluate 2 × 2/1.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 2 mol N₂ × (2 mol NH₃ / 1 mol N₂) = 4 mol.

questions.prompt: For 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O, how many moles of water can 3 mol O₂ form with excess H₂?
hints: Each mole of oxygen supports two moles of water.
The equation gives two water moles per oxygen mole.
Evaluate 3 × 2/1.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The water-to-oxygen ratio is 2:1, giving 6 mol.

questions.prompt: The coefficients 1:3:2 in N₂ + 3 H₂ → 2 NH₃ directly give which ratio?
hints: Keep the amount unit attached to the ratio.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Coefficients count entities and amounts in moles; masses require molar masses.

questions.prompt: For CH₄ + 2 O₂ → CO₂ + 2 H₂O, how many moles of O₂ are required by 2 mol CH₄?
hints: Read oxygen required per methane consumed.
The oxygen-to-methane coefficient ratio is 2:1.
Evaluate 2 × 2/1.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 2 × 2 = 4 mol O₂.

questions.prompt: For 2 Mg + O₂ → 2 MgO, how many moles of MgO can 4 mol Mg form with excess oxygen?
hints: Reduce the product-to-reactant coefficient ratio.
The magnesium and magnesium oxide coefficients are both two.
Equal reactant and product coefficients keep the molar amount unchanged.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The Mg-to-MgO ratio is 2:2, or 1:1.

questions.prompt: A stoichiometric calculation predicts 10 mol of product. When is this theoretical amount reached?
hints: Separate a theoretical calculation from actual reaction yield.
